strapline: Human Rights Watch's post-election ledger, State House answers Khama, Mweetwa's exit explained, Jay Jay Banda's mother goes to court, and Munali Suns make it three

stories.title: Fourteen disappearances and 71 arrests: Human Rights Watch calls for an end to the post-election crackdown, as State House answers Ian Khama and the treason bail ruling nears
stories.excerpt: In a report released on Sunday 1 November, Human Rights Watch says Zambian police and soldiers forcibly disappeared, detained, beat and threatened opposition members, lawyers, journalists and critics around the 13 August election, and that Mutotwe Kafwaya's killing has still not been credibly explained. The report lands amid the row over Ian Khama's description of Hakainde Hichilema as a dictator, three days before the High Court rules on bail for Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 others.

image.label: The post-election ledger
image.caption: Human Rights Watch published its account of Zambia's post-election crackdown on Sunday 1 November 2026; the High Court is due to rule on constitutional bail for 18 treason accused on Thursday 5 November.

body: Human Rights Watch put numbers on the weeks after the election on Sunday. In a report datelined Johannesburg and published on 1 November, the organisation said it had documented 14 cases in August that appear to have been enforced disappearances, with people held for days while the authorities denied having them; 61 cases in which detainees, their lawyers or relatives allege beatings or other violent abuse during arrest or in custody; and 71 cases of opposition members, supporters and critics arrested on charges that may be politically motivated or held for long periods without charge. Eighteen people, it said, have been charged with treason, two of them also with sedition, and treason is not bailable. Six critics had their passports cancelled on 11 September, among them the academic Sishuwa Sishuwa. Seven people the organisation spoke to, including lawyers and a journalist, said they had fled their homes or gone into hiding.

Much of the report retraces events already on the public record and sets them side by side. It records that judicial services were suspended and court premises cordoned off from 24 to 28 August, which the police described as an intelligence-led and preventive measure, and that this coincided with the window for challenging the presidential result. It records the raid on Brian Mundubile's home on 14 August in which the former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was killed, the Inspector General's account that officers met gunfire and returned fire, and the fact that Kafwaya's fate was not confirmed until 19 August after his wife petitioned for habeas corpus. It records the 43 opposition election monitors detained on 14 August whose lawyers said the police denied holding them for eight days, and whose release a Lusaka court ordered on 10 September after 21 days. Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu were arrested on 27 August and are charged with treason and sedition.

body.text: Zambia's government should break this dangerous cycle of repression.
body.attribution: Ashwanee Budoo-Scholtz, deputy Africa director at Human Rights Watch, in the report released on Sunday 1 November

body: The report does not say that Human Rights Watch wrote to the government, and it quotes no reply addressed to it. What it does quote is the government's public response to the UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of assembly and association in September, which the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation called inaccurate, undiplomatic and short of the standards of objectivity expected of UN mandate holders. The ministry said then that membership of an opposition party does not place a person beyond the reach of the law, nor does it convert a criminal suspect into a political detainee, and that Zambia's courts are open to test any claim of unlawful detention. Human Rights Watch's recommendations are a halt to the crackdown, access to lawyers and medical care for detainees, the release of anyone arbitrarily held, accountability for security forces and an independent investigation into the 14 August raid and Kafwaya's death. It also notes that Zambia takes a seat on the UN Human Rights Council for the 2027 to 2029 term.

body.text: does not place a person beyond the reach of the law, nor does it convert a criminal suspect into a political detainee
body.attribution: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, in its September response to the UN Special Rapporteur, as quoted in the Human Rights Watch report of 1 November

body: The report arrived in the middle of an argument Zambia was already having with a neighbour's former president. The Zambian Observer reported on Friday 30 October that Ian Khama had described Hakainde Hichilema as Africa's newest dictator, and on Sunday that he had gone further in an interview with Swaziland News, accusing the government of manipulating elections, persecuting opponents and kidnapping and torturing activists. By Sunday evening State House had answered. The Observer reported that Clayson Hamasaka, the State House communications specialist, said it was hard to understand how Khama could call the President a dictator after visiting State House to hold talks with him, questioned Khama's grasp of the two countries' ties, and alleged that Khama had been among the sponsors of a militia group in Zambia, a claim the Observer noted it could not verify. Earlier, the former vice-president Enock Kavindele had urged Khama to respect Zambia's sovereignty and to back serious allegations with evidence, citing the abolition of the death penalty and the Access to Information Act, and the UPND's media director Mark Simuuwe had questioned the basis of the description. On the other side, the Green Party's Peter Sinkamba said on Sunday that the fairest course would be fresh general elections because, in his words, there is too much explosive tension.

body.text: We have lots of intermarriage between Zambia and Botswana.
body.attribution: Clayson Hamasaka, State House communications specialist, responding to Ian Khama, as reported by the Zambian Observer on Sunday 1 November

body: The next fixed point is Thursday 5 November at 09:00, when a three-judge panel of the High Court in Lusaka, Judges Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga, resumes the constitutional bail application of Mundubile, Zulu and 16 others brought from Mukobeko. Zambia Monitor's account of the last sitting records the court's warning that there would be no further adjournment: the Attorney-General, Mulilo Kabesha, had asked for time to study a 32-paragraph affidavit in reply and 13 paragraphs of skeleton arguments, and the defence lawyer Milner Katolo said the applicants' case rested in part on paragraph 59 of the prosecution manual, which recognises constitutional bail where trial has been delayed. Katolo also raised the health of one applicant, Harry Findlay, who he said had missed appointments with his cardiologist in South Africa.

body.confirmed: Human Rights Watch published its report on 1 November with the figures above; the court closures of 24 to 28 August, the 14 August raid and Kafwaya's death, the 43 monitors' detention and release, and the treason charges against 18 people are matters of public record that the report compiles. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs' September statement is quoted in the report. The bail hearing is set for 5 November at 09:00. Khama's remarks and Hamasaka's reply are as reported by the Zambian Observer.
body.unverified: The individual accounts of beatings, waterboarding and threats in the report rest on the testimony of detainees, relatives and lawyers and on court petitions; the government has not responded to them point by point, and the true number of people detained is unknown because no official total has been published. Hamasaka's allegation that Khama sponsored a militia is unsupported by any published evidence. Khama's remarks have not been published in full by any Zambian outlet.

stories.title: 'I don't have a sense of entitlement': Mweetwa says no MP is owed a ministry, denies planning a new party with other dropped ministers, and stays with the UPND
stories.excerpt: Cornelius Mweetwa spent five years as Minister of Information and Media and chief government spokesman. He kept Choma Central in August but was not among the 30 ministers named this week. In remarks carried by Kalemba and the Zambian Observer on Sunday, he said the President chooses on national interest and skills, that the old Cabinet dissolved with the election, and that talk of him forming a party with other left-out ministers is a political fallacy. News Diggers counts him, Rodney Sikumba and Chipoka Mulenga among the reshuffle's casualties.

image.label: The spokesman steps back
image.caption: Cornelius Mweetwa, Choma Central MP and Minister of Information and Media for five years until the Cabinet dissolved after the August 2026 election, says he is not entitled to a post.

body: For two months the question in Lusaka was when the Cabinet would be named. Once it was, News Diggers observed on Sunday, the question became who had been left out of it. President Hakainde Hichilema unveiled a 30-member Cabinet and ten provincial ministers this week, after Parliament approved enlarging the Cabinet from 25 to 30. The paper's reading is that the delay had been explained in two ways, as time taken to find replacements for ministers who lost their seats, or as room to reward new alliance partners, and that almost nobody had expected ministers who had won their seats and defended the administration to be dropped. Among the former ministers it names as casualties are Cornelius Mweetwa, Rodney Sikumba and Chipoka Mulenga.

Mweetwa has answered the speculation himself. In remarks published by Kalemba and carried by the Zambian Observer on Sunday 1 November, the Choma Central MP said he did not feel entitled to a Cabinet post, that the President's power to appoint ministers rests on national interest, skills and other constitutional considerations, and that no member of Parliament, whether elected, nominated or seated through proportional representation, has an automatic right to a ministry. He rejected the idea that he had been fired or deliberately excluded. The previous Cabinet, he said, dissolved with the general election and a new one had to be built, which he compared to a football coach assembling a new line-up for a new season.

body.text: I don't have a sense of entitlement to be appointed by the President in the midst of members of Parliament.
body.attribution: Cornelius Mweetwa, Choma Central MP and former Minister of Information and Media, as reported by Kalemba and carried by the Zambian Observer on Sunday 1 November

body: The second rumour he addressed was about his loyalties. Mweetwa denied any link to former UPND members or to the opposition, and denied that he planned to form a new party with other former ministers, calling the claims political fallacies. He said he remained committed to the UPND and to the President, thanked Hichilema for the five years he had spent at the Information ministry, and urged party members, including those who lost in August, to stay united behind the Grow Zambia agenda. Neither report says where or on what date he spoke.

body.text: I have one party that I belong to, the UPND, and I have one President that I support.
body.attribution: Cornelius Mweetwa, in the same remarks reported by Kalemba and carried by the Zambian Observer

body: The exit matters beyond one constituency because of the job Mweetwa held. As Minister of Information and Media and chief government spokesperson he was the administration's public voice through its first term. The new ministry list, and who now speaks for the government, were covered in Lusaka Brief's editions of 29 and 30 October; what was missing from them until this weekend was any account from the departed ministers themselves. Mweetwa's is the first.

stories.title: Printed before the withdrawals: the 5 November ballot papers land from Dubai with the Mandevu names still on them, six wards prepare to vote, and Lubinda questions Article 52(6)
stories.excerpt: The Electoral Commission says the ballot papers for Thursday's by-elections arrived at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport on Saturday, a day late, and that the Mandevu papers carry the names of three candidates who have since withdrawn, because printing finished before their letters arrived. Only six wards in five districts will actually poll; the UPND is unopposed in Mandevu, Lumezi North, the Mbala mayoralty and five wards. Given Lubinda says the constitutional amendment that lets a withdrawal end a contest has left voters without a choice.

image.label: Papers without a poll
image.caption: The Electoral Commission of Zambia received the ballot papers for the 5 November 2026 by-elections on Saturday 31 October; those for Mandevu bear the names of candidates who withdrew on 28 October.

body: The ballot papers for Thursday's by-elections exist, and some of them are already obsolete. News Diggers reported on Sunday that the Electoral Commission of Zambia's chief electoral officer, Brown Kasaro, said the consignment arrived from Dubai at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport on Saturday 31 October. It had been expected on Friday, and when it did not come the commission sought an explanation from the printer and the airline. The consignment includes papers for Mandevu constituency bearing the names of candidates who have resigned from the race, because printing was completed before the resignations were communicated to the commission.

Those names are known. Zambia Monitor reported on Friday 30 October that the commission had received letters dated 28 October from Ntazana Musukuma Mutungwa of the Leadership Movement, Daniel Chisenga of the Forum for Democracy and Development and the independent Daniel Daka, each withdrawing with immediate effect. That left Adrian Banda of the UPND as the only validly nominated candidate, and Kasaro's public notice said Banda would be declared duly elected without a poll with effect from 5 November. The notice gave no reasons for the withdrawals and did not say whether the commission had received any formal complaint about the threats and intimidation that some of the candidates alleged.

The commission scheduled 5 November last month for two parliamentary by-elections, Mandevu and Lumezi North, and twelve local government contests, eleven wards and the Mbala mayoralty. Most of them will not need a ballot box. Diggers reported that the UPND stands unopposed in both constituencies, in Mbala, and in five wards, Maako, Siluwe, Upangoma, Mulimambango and Simanvwa, where its candidate was the only one validly nominated. Speaking on Saturday at a training session for polling staff in Lwingishi ward in Mansa, commissioner Zevyanji Sinkala said six wards across five districts would go to the polls on Thursday and that training was under way.

body.text: The clause that ends a contest

body: The former justice minister Given Lubinda has turned the Mandevu outcome into an argument about the constitution. In remarks reported by the Zambian Observer on Sunday, he said the effect of the 2025 constitutional amendment known as Bill 7 was now visible: the amended Article 52(6) allows an election to proceed to a declaration when rival candidates withdraw. He called for a national review of the provision while still encouraging residents to vote. The same mechanism has left the UPND unopposed in Lumezi North, where Diggers reports the opponents also withdrew.

body.text: What is the value of an election if the people are left without a meaningful choice of representatives?
body.attribution: Given Lubinda, former Minister of Justice and former acting president of the Patriotic Front, as reported by the Zambian Observer on Sunday 1 November

body: The governing side reads the withdrawals differently. On Friday, during the Vice-President's Question Time, Mutale Nalumango told MPs that the UPND could consider 2031 already won if opposition parties kept showing political indiscipline, and on Saturday the Citizens First president Harry Kalaba, in a statement reported by the Observer, agreed with her diagnosis, saying opposition leaders had put personal ambition ahead of the public and lacked the unity to offer an alternative government. The Observer also reported that the UPND Alliance, after meeting Nalumango at Government House, plans a nationwide tour to thank voters for August.

stories.title: 'An undisclosed location': Emmanuel Banda's mother asks the High Court to make the police produce her son, as a UPND official says his 2024 escape should count against bail
stories.excerpt: Grace Nampokolwe Banda says she has not seen or heard from her son since he was apprehended in Mozambique in mid-October, that police stations turned her away on 16 October, and that a letter from her lawyers to the Inspector General has gone unanswered. Her habeas corpus application names the Attorney-General as respondent and says no charge, warrant or detention order has been shown to the family. State House has said the former Petauke Central MP faces attempted murder and aggravated robbery charges and will appear before a court.

image.label: Produce the body
image.caption: An application for a writ of habeas corpus over the detention of former Petauke Central MP Emmanuel Jay Banda was filed in the Lusaka High Court at the end of October 2026.

body: A fortnight after the police confirmed they had him, the family of Emmanuel Jay Banda has gone to the High Court to find out where. News Diggers and the Zambian Observer, the latter carrying a Phoenix FM report, both describe an application for a writ of habeas corpus ad subjiciendum filed in Lusaka by the former Petauke Central MP's mother, Grace Nampokolwe Banda. The writ, if granted, orders whoever holds a detainee to produce him before the court and justify the detention. The Attorney-General, Mulilo Kabesha, is named as respondent.

Her affidavit, as both outlets summarise it, says the family has had no access to Banda since his apprehension in Mozambique on 14 October. On 16 October, the day the police publicly confirmed he was in the country and awaiting formal arrest and charge, she says she visited several police stations and was told officers were not ready to allow her to see him. Her lawyers then wrote to the Inspector General of Police, Graphel Musamba, asking for access, and she says the request has not been granted. She describes her son as being held at an undisclosed location without having been formally charged, and says the family has been given no particulars of any offence, no warrant of arrest and no detention order. On that basis the application calls the detention unlawful, arbitrary and unconstitutional and asks the court to compel his custodians to produce him and state the legal basis for holding him.

The government's position was set out before the application was filed. On 20 October State House issued a statement, reported by the Zambian Observer, answering a coalition of 24 civil society and human rights organisations that had questioned the legal basis of Banda's apprehension. Clayson Hamasaka, the State House chief communications specialist, said fleeing across a border does not grant immunity from prosecution, described the apprehension as standard mutual legal assistance, and said Banda was in custody, would appear before a competent court and would receive medical care, access to counsel and his constitutional protections. The statement said he faces High Court charges of attempted murder and aggravated robbery arising from a 2015 incident, that he vanished from lawful custody at Chipata General Hospital on 4 August 2024, and that the government had offered a K2 million reward for his arrest. Those are allegations; Banda has not been tried on them.

On Sunday the UPND's national youth chairman, Gilbert Liswaniso, added the governing party's answer to calls for Banda's release. In remarks reported by the Observer, he said Banda's earlier escape and the year he spent at large should weigh in any bail debate because they raised the risk he would abscond again, that a complaint of prolonged detention was odd when Banda had not yet been brought before a court, and that others had waited longer.

body.text: Mundubile and his friend have been in detention before Jay Jay, so let him wait.
body.attribution: Gilbert Liswaniso, UPND national youth chairperson, as reported by the Zambian Observer on Sunday 1 November

body.confirmed: A habeas corpus application in Mrs Banda's name has been filed in the Lusaka High Court, with the Attorney-General as respondent, as reported by News Diggers and the Zambian Observer. The police confirmed on 16 October that Banda was in the country. State House said on 20 October that he faces attempted murder and aggravated robbery charges and will appear before a court.
body.unverified: Where Banda is being held, whether he has been formally charged since 16 October, and whether the Inspector General has replied to the family's lawyers are not confirmed by any official statement. No hearing date for the application has been reported. The circumstances of his apprehension in Mozambique rest on unnamed sources in the original reports.

stories.title: Drones 'sent to Zambia in error': the Economic and Financial Crimes Court at Chongwe convicts GMX Systems Zambia and two men over under-declared imports, with K2.1 million to pay
stories.excerpt: The Zambia Revenue Authority says the court convicted GMX Systems Zambia Limited, Aminadav Bardavid and Aaron Ngoma of making false representations and importing goods without customs entries. Prosecutors said invoices understated the value of imported drones and that the two men told the ZRA the consignments were meant for a sister company in Israel. The company was fined K30,000 a count and must pay more than K2.1 million in outstanding tax; Bardavid was fined K380,000 and Ngoma K40,000. Six co-accused were acquitted on every count.

image.label: Nineteen counts
image.caption: The Economic and Financial Crimes Court sitting at Chongwe delivered judgment in the GMX Systems Zambia drone importation case on Friday 30 October 2026.

body: A case about drones, invoices and a story of mistaken delivery ended in convictions on Friday. The Economic and Financial Crimes Court, sitting at Chongwe, found GMX Systems Zambia Limited and two individuals, Aminadav Bardavid and Aaron Ngoma, guilty of offences under the Customs and Excise Act, according to a Zambia Revenue Authority statement issued by its corporate communications manager Oliver Nzala and carried by the Zambian Observer on Sunday, and a report in Zambia Monitor the same day. The judgment was delivered on 30 October.

The prosecution's case, as the two reports describe it, had two strands. The first was that the company imported drones using falsified invoices that understated their value and so the tax due, and that some consignments came in without the customs entries the law requires. The second was a representation made to the ZRA: Bardavid and Ngoma, the State alleged, told the authority that the drones had been intended for GMX Systems Limited in Israel and had been shipped to Zambia by mistake, when the real importer was the Zambian company. The charges were framed as making false representations and importing goods without a customs entry under Chapter 322 of the Laws of Zambia.

The company was fined K30,000 on each count, with a warrant of distress to follow if it does not pay, and was separately ordered to pay more than K2.1 million in outstanding taxes. Bardavid was fined K20,000 on each of 19 counts, K380,000 in all, with twelve months' simple imprisonment if he defaults. Ngoma was fined K10,000 on each of four counts, K40,000 in all, with six months in default. Six other people who stood trial alongside them were acquitted on all charges. Neither report names the magistrate or says whether the convicted parties intend to appeal, and neither carries any comment from the defence.

body.text: What the ZRA says it has changed

body: Nzala's statement said the authority had tightened its monitoring of customs declarations to detect fraud, and that the conviction should tell importers that false declarations and misrepresentation bring stiff penalties. It urged importers to lodge the required customs entries, to present accurate invoices and declarations and to pay the taxes due. The authority's statement does not say how the under-declaration was detected or over what period the imports took place.

body.title: The penalties
items: GMX Systems Zambia Limited: K30,000 per count; more than K2.1 million in outstanding taxes; warrant of distress if unpaid
Aminadav Bardavid: K20,000 on each of 19 counts (K380,000); 12 months' simple imprisonment in default
Aaron Ngoma: K10,000 on each of four counts (K40,000); six months' simple imprisonment in default
Six co-accused: acquitted on all counts

body.confirmed: The convictions, the penalties and the acquittal of six co-accused are stated in the ZRA's own release and in Zambia Monitor's report; the judgment date of 30 October is given by the ZRA release.
body.unverified: The presiding magistrate is not named in either report; whether an appeal will be lodged is not reported; the defence's account of the case has not been published.

stories.title: 'Manifestly inadequate': the prosecution asks the Court of Appeal to lengthen Malanji's four years and Yamba's three and to overturn the hotel acquittal, Kalemba reports
stories.excerpt: Kalemba reports, in a story carried by the Zambian Observer on Sunday, that the National Prosecution Authority has filed a cross-appeal against the sentences handed to the former foreign minister Joseph Malanji and the former Secretary to the Treasury Fredson Yamba in September 2025, arguing the trial court should have imposed the statutory maximum, and asking the Court of Appeal to reverse Malanji's acquittal on the Royal Gibson Hotel count. The convictions, sentences and the State's intention to appeal that count are recorded on the NPA's website.

image.label: Both sides appeal
image.caption: The National Prosecution Authority has cross-appealed the September 2025 sentences of Joseph Malanji and Fredson Yamba, Kalemba reported on 1 November 2026.

body: The State wants more time added to two of the most prominent sentences of the Hichilema years, according to a Kalemba report carried by the Zambian Observer on Sunday 1 November. The report says the National Prosecution Authority has filed a cross-appeal in the Court of Appeal against the sentences imposed on Joseph Malanji, the former foreign affairs minister, and Fredson Yamba, the former Secretary to the Treasury, after both men appealed their convictions. It follows an earlier appeal by the Director of Public Prosecutions, Gilbert Phiri, against the sentences and against Malanji's acquittal on one count. No other outlet has yet reported the filing, and this account rests on Kalemba's.

The underlying judgment is a matter of record. The NPA's own website records that in early September 2025 the Economic and Financial Crimes Court, with Chief Resident Magistrate Irene Wishimanga presiding, convicted Yamba on two counts of wilfully failing to follow the procedures for public funds, over transfers of K108,401,197 and K45,800,000 to the Zambian mission account in Turkey, and convicted Malanji on seven counts of possessing property reasonably suspected to be proceeds of crime: a Bell 430 and a Bell 206 helicopter, US$110,000 and US$105,000 in cash, and three houses in Silverest Gardens in Lusaka. He was acquitted on count five, which concerned the Gibson Royal Hotel, the court holding that the hotel predated the financial activity in question; the NPA said at the time that it intended to appeal that acquittal. Malanji was sentenced to four years with hard labour and Yamba to three, to run concurrently. In February 2026 the Lusaka Magistrates' Court refused Malanji bail pending appeal.

Kalemba's account of the cross-appeal gives two grounds. On sentence, the NPA argues that four and three years were manifestly inadequate, wrong in principle and failed to deter or to reflect the gravity of the offences, and that the trial court ought to have imposed the statutory maximum. On the hotel, it argues that the court erred in law. Its case, as reported, is that Malanji's company, Gibson Power Systems, had used the hotel as security for three credit facilities with FNB between 2013 and 2015; that after Malanji travelled to Morocco in October 2020 a deposit of K10,203,000 reached the company's Stanbic account; and that K10 million of it was then used to clear the FNB facilities and the mortgage. Under section 71(1) of the Forfeiture of Proceeds of Crime Act, the NPA says, the State need only show suspicion based on articulable facts, not prove the underlying offence, and it relies on the Supreme Court's decision in The People v Austin Liato. Using suspected proceeds to service a mortgage, it argues, tainted the property even if it was lawfully acquired at first.

body.text: the Trial Court ought to have imposed the statutory maximum
body.attribution: National Prosecution Authority, in its cross-appeal submissions, as quoted by Kalemba in a report carried by the Zambian Observer on 1 November

body: What the defence will say in reply has not been reported. At trial Malanji said his wealth came from Gibson Power Systems and asked for a non-custodial sentence as a first offender, and Yamba's lawyer argued that he had been trying to secure cheaper property for the government and had served ten years as Secretary to the Treasury. No hearing date for the appeals has been published.

body.confirmed: The convictions of September 2025, the sentences, the acquittal on the hotel count and the NPA's stated intention to appeal it are on the National Prosecution Authority's website; the refusal of bail pending appeal in February 2026 is also recorded there.
body.unverified: The filing of the cross-appeal, its grounds and the figures in them are reported by Kalemba alone, via the Zambian Observer; the filing date and any hearing date are not given; the defence has not responded publicly.

stories.title: The 'wandering zone': the Bank of Zambia says a security thread that sits in a slightly different place does not make a banknote counterfeit, and lists the features to check
stories.excerpt: In a public notice on Thursday 29 October the central bank explained that the thread is allowed to move within a defined band during production, so that its extra thickness does not build a ridge in a stack of notes. The eagle image can shift slightly too. The bank's assistant director for communications, Besnat Mwanza, urged people to use several features, the watermark, the see-through register, raised print and colour-shifting ink, rather than the thread alone, and pointed to its free Zambian Banknotes app as a guide, not an authenticator.

image.label: Where the thread may wander
image.caption: The Bank of Zambia's public notice of Thursday 29 October 2026 explains why security threads on genuine notes of the same denomination do not always align.

body: A banknote whose security thread sits a few millimetres from where it sits on the next note is not, by that fact alone, a fake. That was the message of a public notice from the Bank of Zambia on Thursday 29 October, reported by Zambia Monitor that day and by News Diggers on Saturday. The notice was issued by Besnat Mwanza, the bank's assistant director for communications, and its subject was a single feature that some people have been treating as a test of authenticity on its own.

The explanation is mechanical. During production the thread is permitted to shift within a designated area the bank calls the wandering zone. The point of allowing it to wander, Mwanza said, is to spread the thread's extra thickness across a stack: if every thread sat in exactly the same place, the notes would form a ridge when rolled or bundled. As a consequence, threads on genuine notes of the same denomination do not always align exactly, and the eagle image can also appear in slightly different positions. The bank described this variation as neither a defect nor, on its own, an indication that a banknote is counterfeit.

body.text: security threads on genuine banknotes of the same denomination do not always align exactly
body.attribution: Besnat Mwanza, Assistant Director, Communications, Bank of Zambia, in a public notice issued on Thursday 29 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body: The bank's advice is to use several features rather than one, in what it calls a feel, look, feel and check approach. The features that need no equipment, which it calls level one, are the colour-shifting elements, the watermark, the see-through register, where parts of a design on either side of the note line up when held to the light, raised printing that can be felt with a fingertip, and the tactile marks for people with impaired sight. Diggers also reported that the bank promotes a free Zambian Banknotes app on Google Play and the Apple App Store, which it describes as an educational guide to the features and not a tool that automatically authenticates a note.

Diggers filed its report under the K500 note, the highest denomination in circulation, though the bank's notice as reported names no denomination and the principle applies to all of them. The practical effect is for anyone handed a note whose thread sits oddly: the bank's position is that the thread's position alone proves nothing either way, and that the other features settle the question.

stories.title: Thirty-four bales and the bill for burning them: the standards agency seizes used underwear worth K37,350 from a Lusaka shop and restates the 2006 ban on second-hand undergarments
stories.excerpt: The Zambia Compulsory Standards Agency says whistleblowers tipped it off that a Lusaka shop was selling used undergarments, and that officers seized 34 bales valued at K37,350 last week. The shop has been ordered to pay for the consignment's disposal. In a statement on Sunday, the agency's communications manager Brian Hatyoka cited Zambian Standard 559 and Statutory Instrument 120 of 2006, which prohibit the import and sale of used underwear and nightwear, and warned of stern action against traders who ignore them.

image.label: Thirty-four bales
image.caption: The Zambia Compulsory Standards Agency announced on Sunday 1 November 2026 that it had seized 34 bales of used underwear from a Lusaka shop the previous week.

body: The trade in salaula, Zambia's second-hand clothing, is legal, large and visible on every market. One corner of it is not. Used undergarments and nightwear are banned from import and sale, and on Sunday the Zambia Compulsory Standards Agency announced its latest enforcement of the rule: 34 bales of used underwear, valued at K37,350, seized from a shop in Lusaka during the previous week. Zambia Monitor reported the statement on Sunday night and News Diggers on Monday morning.

The agency's communications and public relations manager, Brian Hatyoka, said the operation followed a tip-off from whistleblowers that the shop was selling used undergarments contrary to the law. The shop, which neither report names, was directed to pay the cost of disposing of the consignment. Hatyoka described the seizure as part of ongoing enforcement to protect public health, and warned traders of stern action against the illegal import and sale of used textile products containing undergarments and nightwear, which the agency associates with skin rashes and fungal infections.

body.text: ZS 559 and Statutory Instrument No. 120 of 2006 prohibits the importation and sale of used textile products
body.attribution: Brian Hatyoka, Manager, Communications and Public Relations, Zambia Compulsory Standards Agency, in a statement issued in Lusaka on Sunday 1 November, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body: The legal basis Hatyoka cited is twofold: Zambian Standard 559, the inspection and acceptance criteria for used textile products, and Statutory Instrument 120 of 2006. On the agency's reading, used undergarments and nightwear fall outside what may lawfully be imported and sold, while the wider second-hand clothing trade continues. The agency asked consumers to report any sale of banned items to its nearest office and to buy new undergarments and nightwear. The same statement recorded a visit by the agency to Kasisi Girls Secondary School's annual awards ceremony, where officers urged pupils and teachers to buy from trusted sources and consume safe products.

The value of Sunday's seizure is small. Its purpose, on the agency's own account, is the message to traders who assume the undergarment rule is not policed, and to the whistleblowers whose tip-off the agency credits for this one.

stories.title: Three from three and a 40-point margin: Munali Suns crush Botswana's Dolphins 96–56 at NASDEC, Douglas Kandulu scores 35, and Harare Kings are next on Monday afternoon
stories.excerpt: A day after escaping Ferroviario da Beira by two points, the Lusaka side produced a 40-point win. They led 50–25 at half-time, ran off 16 unanswered points, shot 50 per cent to the Dolphins' 31, and now sit alone at the top of the six-team group on three wins from three. Beira and the Dolphins are both 2–1. The top two go to the Elite 16 in Nairobi from 23 November. The Suns play Harare Kings at 16:00 on Monday and Soweto Panthers after that.

image.label: Three from three
image.caption: Munali Suns beat the Dolphins of Botswana 96–56 at the NASDEC Sports Complex in Lusaka in the Road to BAL 2027 Group E, their third win in three games.

body: If Saturday's win over Ferroviario da Beira was a test of nerve, Sunday's was a statement. Munali Suns beat Botswana's Dolphins Basketball Club 96–56 at the NASDEC Sports Complex in Lusaka, a 40-point margin in Group E of the Road to BAL 2027, and the game that had been billed as a meeting of the group's two unbeaten sides was over by half-time. FIBA's game record has the quarters at 22–14, 28–11, 30–18 and 16–13, a 50–25 lead at the interval, a 16–0 run, and three lead changes.

Douglas Kandulu, who had 21 points, 13 rebounds and five blocks against Beira on Saturday, scored 35 against the Dolphins. The visitors' best was Adrian Breitlauch with 11. The shooting numbers explain the rest: the Suns made half their field goals and 57.9 per cent of their two-point attempts, the Dolphins 31 per cent and 35.6; both sides were poor from distance, at 23.5 and 23.1 per cent. The Dolphins had arrived with wins over Harare Kings and, on Saturday, Bravehearts of Malawi by 78–74, in which Dallan Coleman scored 20.

After three days the Suns are 3–0 and alone at the top with six points. Beira, who beat Harare Kings 98–71 in Sunday's other game, and the Dolphins are both 2–1 on five points; Bravehearts and Harare Kings are 1–2, and Soweto Panthers of South Africa have lost all three. The format FIBA published for this season sends the top two from each first-round group to the Elite 16, with the East Division's Elite 16 to be played in Nairobi from 23 to 29 November and the top two there going to the 2027 Basketball Africa League. The Suns are not yet mathematically through, since Beira, the Dolphins and two others can still finish on four wins, but they hold the head-to-head over both of their nearest rivals.

Monday's programme in Lusaka starts at 10:00 with Beira against Bravehearts, continues at 13:00 with the Dolphins against the Panthers, and finishes at 16:00 with the Suns against Harare Kings, whom Beira beat by 27 on Sunday. Saturday's two-point win over Beira, in which the Suns trailed by ten at half-time, had Elijah Mukelabai with 17 points and eight rebounds and Ofure Ujadughele with 13 points, five assists and five rebounds alongside Kandulu; Beira's Joshua Thomas scored 27. Lusaka Brief reported that game and the opening win over Bravehearts in Sunday's edition.

stories.title: Five draws from six and a goalless Kitwe derby: Zanaco are the only winners of Super League week six, while Fashion Sakala scores and makes two for Al-Fayha
stories.excerpt: Seven goals in six matches on Saturday 31 October, and five of them in Solwezi. Power Dynamos and Nkana shared a 0–0 at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium, Green Eagles, ZESCO United, Red Arrows and FC MUZA all drew blank, and Zanaco's 3–2 at Trident was the only win of the round. MUZA lead Stream A on 11 points, Green Eagles Stream B on the same. In Saudi Arabia, Fashion Sakala scored, set up two more and was named player of the match as Al-Fayha beat Al-Faisaly 4–1.

image.label: Seven goals, six games
image.caption: Matchweek six of the MTN Super League transitional season on Saturday 31 October 2026 produced five draws and a single win, Zanaco's 3–2 at Trident in Solwezi.

body: The Kitwe derby was played in Ndola and produced nothing to separate the sides. Power Dynamos and Nkana drew 0–0 at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium on Saturday 31 October in matchweek six of the MTN Super League's transitional season, and News Diggers' account of the first half has the chances falling to Nkana's Lazarous Kambole, denied by Willard Mwanza after Charles Zulu's cutback in the tenth minute, and to Power's Joshua Mutale, whose shot in the 18th forced a full-stretch save. ZamFoot records that Power have scored four goals this season, the joint-lowest in Stream A with Nchanga Rangers, and that Nkana have now gone two games without a goal since their winning run ended at Konkola.

It was that kind of Saturday. Of six fixtures, five were drawn and four of those finished 0–0: Green Eagles against Kabwe Warriors, ZESCO United against Nkwazi, Red Arrows against Chirundu United and FC MUZA against Nchanga Rangers. Kansanshi Dynamos and NAPSA Stars shared four goals in Solwezi, Nicolas Chisempele and Godfrey Binga scoring for NAPSA and Bebby Musangala and an 89th-minute Joseph Ssemujju penalty for Kansanshi. The only winners were Zanaco, 3–2 at Trident in Solwezi, where Araina Lambert scored twice and Kiala Wa Kiala once against two from Trident's Sam Sikasote.

ZamFoot's tables put FC MUZA top of Stream A on 11 points, a point ahead of Zanaco and Nkana on 10, with Konkola Blades on nine and a game in hand and Power on seven. In Stream B, Green Eagles lead on 11 from ZESCO United on nine, with Chirundu United and Green Buffaloes on eight; Buffaloes had still to play, at home to Mufulira Wanderers, second from bottom, on Sunday, a game Diggers previewed as Wanderers' search for a first win. Mufulira and Mutondo Stars occupy the relegation places in Stream B. Only the winner of each stream goes to the final play-off, which is why a weekend of draws changes less than it would in a conventional league.

The weekend's most productive Zambian was in Saudi Arabia. ZamFoot reports that Fashion Sakala scored Al-Fayha's equaliser with his left foot about seven minutes before half-time, after Abdulrahman Al Safari had put Al-Faisaly ahead in the 30th, then set up Jason in the 66th minute and Hugo Moura in stoppage time as Al-Fayha won 4–1 at Al Majma'ah Sports City Stadium; Ziyad Al-Sahafi had scored the second in the 57th. Sakala was named player of the match and now has three goals and two assists this season, and Al-Fayha climbed to 13th in the Saudi Pro League on 11 points.

analysis.title: What a Human Rights Watch report does and does not change
analysis.body: The report published on Sunday adds little that was not already reported somewhere in Zambia between August and October. Its force is in the compilation: 14, 61, 71 and 18 are numbers that had not been set down together, and they will now be quoted by anyone who wants to describe the post-election period in a sentence. Three things follow. First, the government's position is on the record and consistent: opposition membership is no shield, suspects are not political detainees, and the courts are open. The test of that last claim is Thursday, when the High Court rules on constitutional bail for 18 treason accused after four adjournments. Second, Zambia is due to sit on the UN Human Rights Council for the 2027 to 2029 term, and the report is addressed as much to the governments that elected it as to Lusaka. Third, the Khama exchange shows how the argument is now conducted, by former presidents and spokesmen on social media rather than through the regional channels both sides invoke. Still unknown: the total number detained since August, which no official body has published, and what has been done to investigate Mutotwe Kafwaya's death.

analysis.title: Why a 300-year-old writ is doing the work in the Jay Jay Banda case
analysis.body: Habeas corpus is the oldest instrument a court has for one question: by what authority is this person held? It does not decide guilt and it does not grant bail. It orders the custodian to produce the detainee and explain the legal basis for detention, and it is the remedy a family reaches for when it does not know where someone is. That is the situation Grace Nampokolwe Banda describes, and it is the remedy Mutotwe Kafwaya's wife used in August to learn that her husband was dead. The State's answer is already partly on the record: Banda faces attempted murder and aggravated robbery charges, escaped lawful custody in 2024, and will be brought before a competent court. Both positions can be true at once. A man may be lawfully wanted and still be unlawfully held if no court has been shown a warrant or a detention order, which is what the writ is designed to find out. What to watch is the paperwork rather than the politics: whether the State produces a charge sheet and a date, and how quickly the High Court lists the application. Constitutional limits on detention before charge are, in the end, enforced one writ at a time.

analysis.title: Three wins, two places and the arithmetic of the Elite 16
analysis.body: Munali Suns have done the hard part of a six-team group in three days: beaten the two sides most likely to finish second, one by two points and the other by forty. The arithmetic is not finished. Two places in the Elite 16 go to each first-round group, and with two games left Beira, the Dolphins, Bravehearts and Harare Kings can all still reach four wins, so the Suns are not yet through on paper. In practice, a win over Harare Kings on Monday afternoon would leave them needing nothing from the Panthers game, and they hold the head-to-head over Beira and the Dolphins if it comes to a tie. The group has shown a team with two gears: the composure to come back from ten down against Beira, and the depth to run away from a good Dolphins side the next day. Douglas Kandulu's 35 points on Sunday followed 21 points, 13 rebounds and five blocks on Saturday. The reward for a top-two finish is Nairobi from 23 November, where the top two of the East Division's Elite 16 go to the Basketball Africa League. The thing to watch on Monday is fatigue: the Suns play their fourth group game of the week at 16:00.
